job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Maya Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a structural consultancy in Manchester, checking steel beam calculations for mid-size office and school buildings. Most days I'm on two screens with drawings and a spreadsheet, then once a week I go to a site with my senior, Ruth, to see the real thing. I share a terraced house with two friends from uni. Lately I use an AI chat tool to draft my report summaries, then I rewrite them. After work I go to a climbing gym and ring my mum, who's a nurse and a union rep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overrated. I'd tell my friends it saves me twenty minutes on a report, and that's about it. At work, Ruth would say nothing changes and she'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel fine. My calculations still need a chartered engineer's stamp, and a stamp needs a human. What I do worry about is the housing market. I'm renting in Manchester and my friends are talking about prices like they'll never buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. Keep working towards chartership, which takes about four years of logged experience, and keep my savings in a plain account. I'd maybe use the AI tool a bit more for emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. It's an ordinary life with ordinary stress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the housing market. How does it touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm paying 650 a month for my room and saving a lot, but a deposit on even a small flat near the office is more than I'll save in five years. My parents could add some, but my mum says she doesn't want me to start adult life in their debt. So I'm just watching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the chartered stamp give you that a tool can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It carries legal responsibility. If a floor sags, a named person answers for it. That's why Ruth reads my work line by line, and why I'd feel strange handing the stamp over to a program.

say: The AI chat tool saves me **twenty minutes** on a report, and that's about it.
think: A **chartered stamp** needs a human who answers for the building.
My real worry is **housing prices**, not AI.
do: Keep logging hours toward **chartership**, about four years of experience.
Use the AI tool a little more for **emails**.
feel: I feel **calm**, with ordinary stress about money and flats.
S0.quote: If a floor sags, a named person answers for it.
fieldNote: Her work is protected by **legal responsibility**, so she stays calm.
The only strain she names is **housing**, which her savings do not solve.
She already uses AI lightly and rewrites everything.

steps.text: Log site visits and calculations toward my chartership exam
Use the AI tool for emails and report summaries, then rewrite

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's changing the work, not ending it. I'd tell my friends junior engineers will need to be better reviewers, not faster typists. At work I'd ask Ruth how the firm plans to train juniors if the routine checks go to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the routine checks are how I'm learning. Beams, loads, standard details. If a tool does those, how do I build judgement? I might become someone who approves answers I never worked out, which scares me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to keep a set of calculations that juniors do by hand each month, as practice. I'd learn the new design software the firm buys, and I'd study for chartership faster. I'd also join the company's staff forum and ask about training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also curious. I like the idea of getting better tools, I just want to keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said approving answers you never worked out scares you. When would that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably in my third or fourth year, when I'm sent a pile of automated checks and told to sign off by Friday. I'd have to trust something I can't see inside. I'd say out loud that I want to redo a sample by hand, and I hope I'd be allowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would help you with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth, I think. She did her first years with a slide rule and she's always saying you can't judge a number you couldn't have guessed. My mum would say form a group of juniors and ask together, which is her answer to everything.

say: The work changes, and juniors must become **better reviewers**, not faster typists.
I'd ask Ruth how the firm will train juniors.
think: Routine checks are how I learn, so automating them risks my **judgement**.
I fear signing off answers I never worked out.
do: Ask the firm to keep a monthly set of **hand calculations** for juniors.
Join the **staff forum** and push for training.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but curious about better tools.
S1.quote: You can't judge a number you couldn't have guessed.
fieldNote: Her worry is **learning**, not losing the job.
Ruth is a mentor figure, and her mother's union habits shape her answer.
She still wants the better tools.

steps.text: Ask my firm to keep monthly hand calculations for juniors
Learn the new design software the firm buys
Book the chartership interview a year earlier

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is brutal. I'd say we need training funds and income support ready, and I'd say it online to people who'd listen. At work I'd go to Ruth and ask what the plan is, even if the answer is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of junior desk work is gone within two years. The stamp might hold longer, because insurers and regulators move slowly, but firms might hire fewer people to hold it. I'd be anxious about being the cheaper person who's let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every spare pound and spend a few evenings a week learning what the AI tools do on my own project files. I'd talk to my mum about a union for engineers. I'd also think about whether to take on site work, since site visits are the one part a machine can't do for three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit angry that no one planned for it. But I'm not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the site work is something a machine can't do for three more years. Why does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it gives me a place to be useful while the desk work changes. If I'm the one who walks the site, spots the badly poured slab, talks to the foreman, that matters in 2031. I'd ask to do more site visits than the other juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm still earning well and I'm saving. But I'd ask her how she's seen nurses handle big changes in hospitals, because they've gone through reorganisations before. She'd say stick together and don't take the first offer.

say: Two years is brutal, so training funds and **income support** must be ready.
I'd ask Ruth what the plan is, even if it's nothing.
think: A lot of junior desk work could go within two years.
Firms might hire fewer people to hold the **stamp**, and I could be let go.
do: Save every spare pound and learn the AI tools on my own **project files**.
Ask for more **site visits**, the part machines reach last.
feel: I feel **frightened** and a bit angry that no one planned, but not frozen.
S2.quote: If I'm the one who walks the site, spots the badly poured slab, talks to the foreman, that matters in 2031.
fieldNote: Her plan is to stay **physical site**, where robots arrive later.
Her mother's nursing experience gives her a model for facing big change.
Savings keep her at anxious instead of alarmed.

steps.text: Ask Ruth to put me on more site visits than other juniors
Save 1,200 a month and keep a year of rent in reserve
Run the AI tools on old project files to see what they get wrong
Talk to an engineers' union about joining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to prepare, but only if people actually do. I'd tell friends to start now. I'd also say the profession's bodies should be setting training standards, not waiting for firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think by 2031 the pure design work is mostly done by machines, and engineers will be the ones who check the design against reality. I'd like to be the person who's been on a hundred sites by then. The part that worries me is that firms might hire half the graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish chartership in the first two years, then try to move into site supervision or client-facing work. I'd keep learning the AI tools so I can tell when they're wrong. And I'd save enough for a flat deposit, because I'm not sure about prices after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it feels like something I can work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms might hire half the graduates. What do you say to the graduate behind you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get the site experience early and learn the tools. And don't hide away in the design office. People who can talk to builders are going to be gold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the flat deposit really worth the effort, given the uncertainty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the one thing I can do that doesn't depend on a boss. If my job changed, owning something would help, as long as I'm not stretched. I'd pick something small and I'd keep the savings above six months.

say: Five years is enough to prepare, but only if people **start now**.
Professional bodies should set training standards, not wait for firms.
think: By 2031 pure design is mostly machine work, and engineers **check against reality**.
Firms might hire half as many graduates.
do: Finish **chartership** in two years and move toward site supervision.
Save for a small **flat deposit** and keep six months in reserve.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but it feels like something I can work on.
S3.quote: People who can talk to builders are going to be gold.
fieldNote: She turns the warning into a **career plan** that moves toward people and sites.
She worries about the next graduates, not just herself.
The flat deposit is her one idea of independence from a boss.

steps.text: Move toward site supervision and client meetings
Save a small flat deposit and keep six months in reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a good run. I'd say people should keep learning and not panic. At work I'd say let's plan the next decade of training for juniors, because by then the job will look different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be around 32, probably a chartered engineer with a team. The job will have changed, but ten years is long enough for me to change with it. I'd worry about the juniors who come in around 2034 and find no entry-level work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, buy a flat in about five years, and probably have a child by then. I'd learn the tools as they appear. I'd also go to the union for engineers and ask what a fair apprenticeship looks like in an AI world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. There's time to think and even enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a child. How does that fit with a changing job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want that security under me before a baby, which is why the ten years suits me. A flat and some savings mean I could take a year of leave and not panic. My mum says have your kids when you're ready, and not when the economy says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair apprenticeship look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years where juniors do real work with a mentor, a tool they're taught to question and a pay rise that isn't up to the boss's mood. Something written down, not luck. I'd push for it in my own firm once I'm senior.

say: Ten years is a good run, so people should keep learning and **not panic**.
I'd propose planning training for juniors for the next decade.
think: At 32 I'd be a **chartered engineer** with a team, with the job changed but me too.
I worry about **juniors** arriving around 2034 with no entry-level work.
do: Buy a **flat** in about five years and think about starting a family.
Push for a **fair apprenticeship** written down in my firm once I'm senior.
feel: I feel **settled**, with time to think and even enjoy it.
S4.quote: Two years where juniors do real work with a mentor, a tool they're taught to question and a pay rise that isn't up to the boss's mood.
fieldNote: Ten years gives her space to plan a **family and a flat**.
Her worry is for the **next generation of juniors**, not herself.
She'd use her seniority to make training fairer.

steps.text: Buy a flat in about five years
Plan a year of leave around having a child
Push my firm to write down a fair apprenticeship for juniors

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because two years is almost no time to retrain or for the profession to react. What would help is training funds that juniors can use, rules that someone must stay accountable for a design, and employers that keep hiring real graduates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd add that people assume young engineers are all excited about AI. I use it, but I'm cautious, and I want the older engineers to keep teaching us. If they retire and the machines replace the training, we lose something.

headlineQuote: My mum says have your kids when you're ready, and not when the economy says.
portrait: Maya is a **22-year-old** civil engineer at a Manchester consultancy, top of her class with two internships.
She uses AI tools **now and then** and rewrites everything, trusting the chartered stamp.
Her mum is a nurse and union rep, and Maya leans on that **collective habit**.
She stays calm when a human stamp is needed, and turns **anxious** when time is short.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries her most, because there's almost no time to retrain or react.
whatWouldHelp: **Training funds** for juniors, accountability rules for designs and employers who keep hiring graduates.
